name: Yusuf Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Yusuf. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say is tied to your name. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the retentions team at a mobile phone network. When someone rings up to cancel their contract, they get put through to me, and my job is to keep them. I'll offer a better deal, more data, a cheaper handset, whatever I'm allowed. I'm good at it because I listen first, and I'm proud of my numbers. What wears me down is the targets changing every quarter.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about your life outside work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm twenty-seven and engaged to Amina, the wedding's next August. I still live at my parents' place to save, so I've got over a year's pay put away for the wedding and a deposit. My dad runs a tyre and exhaust garage on the industrial estate, and I help him on Saturdays. Friday prayers, football, family, that's my week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I always knew it was talk. These tech firms sell big promises to get investors' money. I'd say it to the lads on the team and my dad, nothing online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep doing what I do. Nobody wants to talk to a computer when they're angry about their phone bill. They want a person who can actually give them something. Maybe the computer does the paperwork after the call, which is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Keep my numbers up, keep saving for the wedding and the house, and help Dad on Saturdays. I wouldn't touch the AI stuff unless I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. That's the world I'm planning for anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't touch AI unless you had to. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't need it. My manager, Craig, keeps telling me to use the suggestion box on the screen, and I ignore it because my own words work better. Customers can hear when you're reading something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything weighing on you, apart from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding costs, honestly, and house prices. But I've saved properly, so I'm not worried, just careful.

say: I'd say AI was always **just talk** from tech firms chasing investors.
I'd say it to my **team and dad**, not online.
think: Angry customers want **a person** who can actually give them a deal.
AI doing **after-call paperwork** would be fine by me.
do: Keep my **retention numbers** up on the team.
Keep saving for the **wedding and house**.
Keep helping Dad at the **garage on Saturdays**.
feel: **Settled**, because this is the world I'm planning for anyway.
S0.quote: Nobody wants to talk to a computer when they're angry about their phone bill. They want a person who can actually give them something.
fieldNote: Yusuf takes **pride in his numbers** and his own way of talking to customers.
He ignores the **on-screen suggestions** his manager pushes, a firm resistant streak.
Strong **savings** from living at home make him feel safe.

steps.text: Keep hitting monthly retention targets on the phone network team
Keep saving for the August wedding and a house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it at work quietly, that the company is chasing cheap over good. Customers will leave if they can't get a person. I'd not complain loudly, though, I'm not a moaner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me more than I'd say. If the network lets a bot offer the deals, retentions doesn't need ten of us, maybe three. The three will be the ones good with the new system. That isn't me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my dad about working at the garage more, maybe going part time there. I'd hold off on buying a house until the job's clear, and keep the wedding modest. I'd probably sit the company's training on the new system, but only because they'd make me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in my gut. Like when the targets change and you don't know if you'll hit them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd take the training only because they'd make you. Isn't that the thing that might keep you in the three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Amina would say that, she's always telling me to stop being stubborn. I'd probably do it, but I'd be doing it with my arms crossed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Amina's family about the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I've got savings and a trade with my dad if I need it. Her father's a careful man, he'd want to know I can provide. I'd tell him straight that the phone job might not last.

say: I'd say quietly that the company is chasing **cheap over good**.
I'd warn that customers will **leave** if they can't reach a person.
think: A deal-making bot means retentions needs **three of us**, not ten.
The three kept will know the **new system**, which isn't me.
do: Talk to Dad about **part-time work** at the garage.
Hold off on **buying a house** until the job is clear.
Keep the **wedding modest** to protect savings.
feel: Uneasy in my gut, like **missing a target** you can't control.
S1.quote: If the network lets a bot offer the deals, retentions doesn't need ten of us, maybe three. The three will be the ones good with the new system.
fieldNote: Yusuf's public line is **quieter** than his private worry.
He admits his **stubbornness** about AI may cost him a place on the smaller team.
His fallback is **family**: his father's garage and his own savings.

steps.text: Ask Dad about part-time shifts at the tyre and exhaust garage
Put off buying a house until the phone job is clear
Cut the wedding guest list and budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when nobody puts the brakes on. I don't want the government running everything, but somebody should have slowed it down. At the mosque everyone would be talking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job is finished, quickly. Talking people into staying is just words and offers, and if a computer can do any thinking work, it can do that. My dad's garage is hands-on, so it gives me about three years after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the phone job in the first year and join my dad full time, learning tyres, exhausts and brakes properly. I'd keep the savings untouched and still get married, because you don't put your life on hold for a computer. We'd live with my parents for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I keep thinking about the wedding and whether I'm walking into marriage with no job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still get married. Did you think about waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Amina and I have waited long enough, and our families are ready. Marriage isn't a business decision. The house can wait, the wedding can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And when robots come for garage work, around 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I don't know. My dad would probably sell up. Maybe I'd do something in the community, the mosque always needs people. I'm not the type to sit on benefits.

say: I'd say this is what happens when nobody **puts the brakes** on.
I don't want **government running everything**, but someone should have slowed it.
think: Retentions is **words and offers**, so my job is finished quickly.
My dad's garage gives me about **three years** before robots arrive.
do: Leave the phone job and join Dad's **garage full time**.
Keep **savings untouched** and still marry Amina in August.
Live with my **parents** for a few years after the wedding.
feel: Alarmed, worried about **walking into marriage** with no job.
S2.quote: Marriage isn't a business decision. The house can wait, the wedding can't.
fieldNote: Yusuf's **faith and family** decide what he won't change: the wedding goes ahead.
He uses the **robot gap** by moving fully into hands-on garage work.
He rejects **benefits**, preferring community and family support.

steps.text: Quit the phone network and work full time at Dad's garage
Keep all savings untouched as a cushion
Marry Amina in August and live with his parents

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been warned, so people should get a trade while they can. That's what my dad would say too. I'd tell the younger lads on the team to look at apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I have a few years to plan, but the phone job ends either way. I'd be thirty-two when it hits. That's young enough to learn a trade properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on retentions for two more years while saving everything I can, then move to the garage. I'd do the motor vehicle course at the college on Saturdays instead of just helping. We'd marry next August and rent a small place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but not frantic. It's like seeing a storm coming from far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy the house in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd rather rent than have a mortgage hanging over us when my income's changing. My dad never had a mortgage until he was forty and he did fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the garage when robots come, around 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a long way off. Cars might all be electric by then and need less work anyway. I'd worry about it when I'm closer.

say: I'd tell people to **get a trade** while they still can.
I'd point the younger lads towards **apprenticeships**.
think: The phone job **ends either way**, but I'd have years to plan.
At **thirty-two** I'd still be young enough to learn a trade.
do: Stay on retentions **two more years** and save everything I can.
Take the college's Saturday **motor vehicle course**.
Rent a small place after marrying, **not buy**.
feel: Worried but not frantic, like a **storm** seen far off.
S3.quote: I'd rather rent than have a mortgage hanging over us when my income's changing.
fieldNote: Yusuf's **resistance** shows in his refusal to think past 2034.
He'd use the time for a **traditional apprenticeship** route.
His father's **no-mortgage** history shapes his money choices.

steps.text: Stay on the retentions team two more years and save hard
Take the Saturday motor vehicle course at the college
Rent a small flat after the wedding instead of buying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who doesn't prepare can't blame anyone else. I believe that. People need to stand on their own feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine, mostly. I can stay on the phones for years, buy the house, and move to the garage when it makes sense. Maybe I'd even take it over from my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the phone job and keep saving. We'd buy a small house after the wedding. Then in a few years I'd start taking over the garage, maybe open a second bay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more settled. There's time to do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you could stay on the phones for years. Would you try the new tools at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they'd help me keep the job longer, maybe. But I'm not going to pretend to love them. I'll do what I need to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the end, when robots get good at garage work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By then I'd be nearly forty, with a house and maybe kids. I'd want the garage to be worth something to sell. My family has always done it that way: build something and hand it on or sell it.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty, and people must stand on their own feet.
Anyone who doesn't prepare **can't blame** anyone else.
think: I can stay on the phones for years and **buy the house**.
I might eventually **take over** the garage from Dad.
do: Keep the **phone job** and keep saving.
Buy a **small house** after the wedding.
Start taking over the garage and maybe open a **second bay**.
feel: **Uneasy** but more settled, with time to do it properly.
S4.quote: My family has always done it that way: build something and hand it on or sell it.
fieldNote: Ten years lets Yusuf follow his **family's path** without rushing.
He'd use new tools only **if forced**, still resistant.
He thinks in terms of **building a business** to hand on or sell.

steps.text: Keep working on the retentions team and saving each month
Buy a small house with Amina after the wedding
Take over Dad's garage and add a second bay

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of the wedding. Starting married life with no job isn't how I pictured it. What would help is apprenticeships for people like me, paid ones, not more handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what families can do. My dad's garage is my safety net. Not everyone has a dad with a garage, and the people who don't are the ones I'd worry about.

headlineQuote: My dad's garage is my safety net. Not everyone has a dad with a garage, and the people who don't are the ones I'd worry about.
portrait: Yusuf is a **27-year-old** retentions agent at a mobile network, proud of his numbers.
He's engaged to Amina, lives with his parents and has over **a year saved**.
He never uses AI tools and believes customers want **a real person**.
He moves from calm to **alarmed**, with his father's **tyre garage** as his escape route.
He favours **apprenticeships and family** over government handouts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd start married life with no job.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for people like him, not more handouts.
